body_references.text: The decision map in @fig-master-loop brings these questions together. It follows how we notice and interpret information, construct options, anticipate consequences, and judge how much those consequences matter. Once we choose and commit, the resulting outcomes give us an opportunity to learn.
The route in @tbl-long-form-journey expands from individual choices to interaction and the design of decision processes. Each step adds a question that the earlier parts help us answer.

When you use the map, keep the four terms in @tbl-navigation-vocabulary distinct: interpreting what something means, predicting an outcome, forming an expectation, and deciding how much the outcome matters answer different questions.
Use @tbl-reading-routes to choose a route that fits your question. The focused routes connect related chapters without requiring you to read the whole book first.

The committee needs to improve its hiring process, but it cannot diagnose a failure merely by restating what a good decision would look like. It must identify how the actual judgment departed from that standard and what could change it. The normative, descriptive, and prescriptive perspectives in @tbl-three-questions separate these tasks and set different standards of success.

The distinction between a standard and an explanation now gives the committee a practical task. Use @tbl-hiring-loop to identify where its process is vulnerable, then select a response aimed at that difficulty. Adding another interview will not settle a disagreement about priorities, just as agreeing on priorities will not repair unreliable evidence.

Compare changes in representation, options, and the path to action in @tbl-seven-context-examples. The subscription comparison comes from Ariely (2008) and related attraction-effect experiments (Huber et al., 1982). Stated agreement in Johnson and Goldstein (2003) and deceased donation in Dallacker et al. (2024) are different outcomes. The reported increase in clicks followed a bundled redesign (Land & Yuan, 2012).[^ch01-ad-redesign]

The separate columns in @tbl-prediction-value keep forecasts open to an evidence check and values open to discussion. A weight such as “health: 30 percent” is hard to interpret until the relevant range and trade-off are specified, and uncertainty should remain visible in the entries.

To assess a proposed question or test, list its plausible answers and the action that would follow each. Then compare the expected benefit of acting on the answer with the cost of obtaining and using it. In @tbl-information-decision-branches, the pilot and timing question can redirect action; the diagnostic test, as specified, cannot.

A second experiment asked whether distraction could spread. Different students took paper notes, seated either with or without a view of multitasking laptops used by researchers posing as students. Seeing those screens also reduced comprehension. @fig-laptop-distraction shows the two comparisons: competing activity can affect both its user and nearby learners.

The scenes in @fig-sensory-windows show what different sensory systems make available. A pit viper can detect infrared radiation from a warm animal through heating of a sensitive membrane in its facial pit (Gracheva et al., 2010). A bee can detect ultraviolet contrasts on petals that look uniformly coloured to us; the flower pair uses false colour to reveal such a pattern (Chittka & Menzel, 1992; Koski & Ashman, 2014). Some elephant calls include frequencies below 20 Hz, the conventional lower boundary of human hearing (Payne et al., 1986). European robins can use the inclination of Earth's magnetic field to orient their migratory headings (Wiltschko & Wiltschko, 1972, 2005).

At the organizational level, meetings and dashboards put these design choices into practice by allocating attention before any participant begins to reason. @tbl-attention-architecture traces five design choices from what they make visible to what can be missed:
Use @tbl-05-1 to match the redesign to the failure: protecting focus addresses distraction, whereas an issue excluded from the agenda needs a route into discussion.

Look at @fig-recognition-two-tone for a few seconds. What, if anything, do the patches represent? Write down your first interpretation, or note that you cannot yet find one. The grayscale version appears after the core examples, where you can compare what you saw before and after the reveal.

Before looking below, recall your first interpretation of @fig-recognition-two-tone. Now examine the grayscale image in @fig-recognition-grayscale, then cover it or turn back to the opening image. Does the same arrangement of black and white look different?

Read the middle symbol in each row of @fig-context-b13-demonstration. Its shape is identical in the two rows, but the neighbors invite different readings. The surrounding numbers make a numerical sequence relevant; the letters make the alphabet relevant. Both are familiar structures learned through experience. Context makes one interpretation easier to access. How much of your reading came from the mark, and how much came from its setting?

Consider the unfinished sentence **“At the bank, she…”** After a paragraph about fishing, *cast her line* would be a plausible continuation. After a paragraph about opening a savings account, *asked about interest rates* would fit better. The words to be continued are unchanged, but the setting changes what a good answer would be. Like the neighbors around the ambiguous symbol in @fig-context-b13-demonstration, surrounding information guides interpretation. This is useful when context clarifies a task; it becomes consequential when an assumption embedded in the question quietly guides the answer.

Look first at the isolated light on the left in @fig-traffic-light-color-context. What color would you call it? Now look at the upper lamp on the right. Both show the same lens, but only the right supplies its familiar setting. Does recognizing the traffic signal make the upper light seem redder?

The first row of @tbl-two-meanings-prediction asks, in effect, **“What is producing the signals I am receiving?”** The second asks **“What is likely to happen if this option is chosen?”** Both use prior information and uncertainty, but they predict different objects and are evaluated against different evidence. In a hiring interview, interpreting a quiet answer as thoughtfulness is an inference about what just happened; predicting reliable future work is a further claim.

Predictive-processing models differ in their scope and implementation. Some model aspects of attention through precision assignment (Feldman & Friston, 2010), but precision and attention are not interchangeable. The return path through action and sampling in @fig-predictive-processing-decision also explains why a smaller prediction error need not mean a better account of the world: the system may have sampled only evidence its model already explains.

Before looking below, recall your first interpretation of @fig-recognition-two-tone. Now examine the grayscale image in @fig-recognition-grayscale, then cover it or turn back to the opening image. Does the same arrangement of black and white look different?

Before reading the caption, name the animal in @fig-duck-rabbit-context. Then try to find another animal without rotating the image. The challenge is to reorganize the same marks, not discover a second hidden drawing.

In @fig-perception-context-lab, the paired shafts, centre circles, and grey patches are physically identical within each comparison. The surrounding geometry or luminance changes their appearance. Measuring the target can correct the judgment without necessarily turning off the impression.

Watch the upper mask in @fig-hollow-face-illusion, then compare it with the featureless hollow surface below. Does the face seem to bulge toward you? Does its apparent shape change as it turns? Try separating what you **know about the shape** from what you **see**.

The contrasting loops in @tbl-self-fulfilling-self-defeating make “Was the forecast right?” an incomplete review question. Ask also: **Through what actions did the forecast change exposure, effort, resources, or other people’s responses?** A label such as “promising” or “unreliable” may influence the conditions under which the person will next be judged. The review must distinguish that treatment from evidence about performance under other conditions.

The pathways in @tbl-08-expectation-pathways can operate together. A manager who withholds decision authority changes what an employee can try, while interpreting the resulting work can still involve selective attention. Record the responsibility delegated alongside the predicted performance. A forecast can help bring about the outcome, or it can prompt a change that prevents it (Merton, 1948; Harris & Rosenthal, 1985; Kirsch, 1985).

Support also has to be credible. Telling employees they are trusted while retaining every decision gives them conflicting instructions. @tbl-08-1 pairs each setting’s pathway with the support or safeguard it requires, from balanced risk information in medicine to credible authority and resources in management. A disappointing result may reflect the task, material constraints, discrimination, or luck; it cannot be used to conclude that the person failed to believe strongly enough.

The studies in this chapter distinguish what people expect from what that expectation helps bring about. The practical recording tool in @tbl-consequence-forecast keeps both questions visible. Its product-launch figures are illustrative assumptions, not measured success rates.

Value can begin to bend before deliberate comparison. Evaluative-priming studies, for example, measure whether a positive or negative cue changes response speed to a later target. Such latency differences can reveal rapid valence activation shaped by task, semantic relatedness, attention, and goal relevance (Giner-Sorolla et al., 1999; Klauer et al., 2016; Spruyt et al., 2018). Chapter 13 examines accessibility and priming in detail; here @tbl-automatic-evaluation-stages separates the initial appraisal from the broader valuation and action it may influence.

The word “preference” can also hide differences between enjoying an outcome, feeling drawn toward it, judging it worth choosing, and acting from habit. The distinctions in @tbl-value-is-not-one-thing will matter when an action continues even though it brings little pleasure:

The evidence requirements in @tbl-contextual-cues-and-waiting show why arousal or neural reward responses alone cannot establish a change in intertemporal choice. A behavioral shift may instead reflect perceived time or a starting-point bias toward immediate rewards. The designs help distinguish these pathways.
Apply @tbl-07-1 to the strongest reason for accepting the invitation. A feeling may identify a benefit worth valuing, but a claim about what will happen still needs independent evidence.

The sequence in @fig-choice-blindness-swap uses illustrated faces to show how the face experiment separates the original selection from the option presented for explanation. Its interest lies in the reasons offered for an undetected substitution: a participant can discuss details of the rejected face as though they motivated the choice (Johansson et al., 2005).

Ask what the reviewer can claim to have anticipated in @tbl-narrator-record. A decision journal preserves the original alternatives, assumptions, forecasts, values and reasons. An appended entry checks each against the outcome. The May finish does not establish that the original plan could have delivered it. [Chapter 41](41-decision-hygiene.qmd#what-a-decision-journal-is) develops the same record for an organization. [Appendix F](../appendices/appendix-c-portable-course-tools.qmd#one-page-decision-journal) provides the portable template.

Use @tbl-rationalization-detector to turn a story into claims that can be compared with evidence. A persuasive answer to every question is still a hypothesis; it earns support when it explains observations that plausible rivals do not.
The paired judgments in @tbl-process-outcome-review show why a favorable result does not excuse a poor process, and an unfavorable result does not condemn a sound one:

The Stroop task lets you experience competing responses. In @fig-stroop-interference-lab, name the **ink colour**, rather than read the printed word. Move left to right at an even pace, starting with the neutral row and then the conflict row. Reading is so practiced that a colour name printed in a different colour supplies a competing response before the instructed answer is ready. People are typically slower and more error-prone when controlled attention must resolve this conflict between a fluent but task-irrelevant response and the current goal (Stroop, 1935).

In @fig-daughter-finger-counting, my three-year-old daughter uses her fingers as an external counting tool to compute 4 + 1. She had to hold the problem in mind, map numbers onto fingers, and inspect the result. The same answer later can arrive without visible counting. With suitable practice and feedback, some components of an initially effortful, rule-guided activity can become faster and more automatic.
The contrasts in @tbl-04-1 summarize common processing features, not two kinds of person or two fixed locations in the brain.

The same distinction matters when deciding what deserves protection. In @fig-affect-panda-sea-star, notice which species first draws your concern and what features prompt that response. This is a judgment about appeal; deciding how to allocate conservation funds requires evidence about what each intervention would accomplish.

Use @tbl-10-1 to match the check to the shortcut, while keeping open whether a vivid case reveals something the broader record misses. One near miss cannot estimate an accident rate, but it can reveal a new failure pathway. Intuition can suggest a hypothesis; evidence must then establish how much weight it deserves.
Check your predictions against @tbl-two-triples.

Confirmation, motivated reasoning, and self-serving attribution differ in what they protect, but they share a process risk: search, interpretation, and explanation become easier in the direction of a preferred conclusion. The corrections in @tbl-13-1 make “be objective” testable by specifying what must be compared: rival predictions, evidence thresholds, causal standards, or situational explanations.

@fig-subscription-decoy is memorable because the decoy received no choices, yet its removal changed what people selected. Huber et al. (1982) provide the experimental foundation for this attraction effect.

The hiring case shows why the correction must match the comparison. More careful adjustment cannot create an estimate independent of the anchor; more discussion of the candidate cannot supply a missing work sample. @tbl-14-1 matches the diagnosed problem to a practical change informed by research on debiasing (Larrick, 2004).

Imagine holding a window frame in front of you and judging a neighborhood through its opening. Look first at the three upper frames in @fig-framing-three-windows. The buildings might suggest a densely built district, the trees an extensive park, and the falling droplets a rainy street. The lighter surroundings illustrate these possible reconstructions. Now look below: the three selected views belong to one neighborhood. The wider scene reveals a lawn sprinkler outside the third frame, explaining the droplets without rain. The contents of each frame have stayed exactly the same; what differs above is the wider scene imagined around them.
The window metaphor in @fig-framing-three-windows suggests a second move: widen the view. The wider scene can test what we have imagined beyond the available evidence.

The rows of @tbl-disease-framing preserve the same final possibilities and probabilities. The first makes a guaranteed rescue focal; the second foregrounds a guaranteed loss. [Chapter 17](17-prospect-theory.qmd#the-prospect-theory-model) uses the example to examine how reference points and probability weighting can produce that pattern.

In @fig-assumed-choice-eggs, adding “no egg” restores an option hidden by the second question. “Would you prefer delivery this week or next week?” similarly treats purchase as settled. These are cases of **substantive reframing**: the inquiry changes which options, objectives, or causal accounts receive consideration. They deserve scrutiny even though they are not tests of equivalent numerical descriptions.

That first result could reflect a changed report without a changed memory. A second experiment therefore asked about broken glass one week later. There was none in the film, yet **16 of 50** students previously asked about “smashed” reported seeing it, compared with **7 of 50** asked about “hit” and **6 of 50** controls who received no speed question. @fig-wording-memory-study-redraw keeps the immediate estimate and later report separate.

The same care applies in management. A label such as “rightsizing” should not obscure job losses, and calling a workload a “stretch goal” does not establish that it is sustainable. The safeguards in @tbl-15-1 follow what the frame changed: restate equivalent quantities, reopen missing alternatives, or test an implied cause.

Read the evidence column in @tbl-16-1 before carrying a finding across outcomes: faster processing, a changed judgment, and changed behavior are different claims. Motivation, incentives, constraints, identity, and competing cues shape the path between them.
**Predict first.** In each pool, which group supplies more positive screens? Read the positive counts in @fig-probability-judgment-map and add the two routes before dividing.
In @fig-monty-hall-two-hosts, trace the rule for the host who knows where the car is. If there are two available goat doors, assume the host chooses between them at random.

Return to the branch manager. If the bad quarter was two standard deviations below average and the same illustrative correlation of 0.40 applied, the model would predict the next quarter at 0.8 standard deviations below average without any managerial change. That is a visible recovery of 1.2 standard deviations. @fig-regression-conditional-shrinkage shows the corresponding geometry. The recovery can be real while its attribution to the rescue plan remains unproven. Compare the branch with similarly troubled branches, examine several earlier periods, and identify which changes the manager actually introduced. That makes room for a managerial effect while accounting for the recovery that might have happened anyway.
Each requires a different comparison, as @tbl-confidence-calibration shows. Asking a confident person to “think harder” supplies none of them.

The **planning fallacy** is this tendency to underestimate how long a task will take. A plausible story of the remaining steps can crowd out experience of earlier delays (Buehler et al., 1994; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Underestimating the time needed can express overestimation of what one can accomplish; an unduly narrow completion window also expresses overprecision. It is an application of the errors in @tbl-confidence-calibration, rather than a fourth form of overconfidence.
@fig-confidence-accuracy separates the two trajectories: confidence rose at every stage, while accuracy fluctuated within a much narrower range.

The dated entries in @tbl-probability-forecast-ledger matter because memory rounds forecasts toward outcomes. “We knew it might fail” can describe almost any vague prior statement. A dated number, event definition, and update rule allow learning to survive hindsight.

Start on the chord at average wealth 50 in @fig-risky-decision-map. The expected utility there is 5. Moving horizontally to the utility curve reaches the sure wealth that gives the same utility. That comparison distinguishes expected utility from utility evaluated at average wealth.

A risk-preference measure seems useful because it could help predict choices beyond the task. Yet changing the task can change a person’s classification. Before using that label in another setting, we need to identify what the task measured. @tbl-risk-elicitation pairs each task with what it can reveal and what complicates the inference. A model maps choices back to a parameter, but comprehension, probability format, reference point, response mode, and noise can also affect the result.

In @fig-prospect-theory-map, first locate the reference point and see which part of the value curve the outcome occupies. Then compare the decision weight with the objective probability. The two functions jointly shape the risky-choice predictions summarized in @tbl-fourfold-risk-attitudes.

In @fig-prospect-theory-map, first locate the reference point and see which part of the value curve the outcome occupies. Then compare the decision weight with the objective probability. The two functions jointly shape the risky-choice predictions summarized in @tbl-fourfold-risk-attitudes.

We can now combine the two influences. Curvature describes the value of the possible gain or loss; weighting describes the influence of its probability. Crossing the gain–loss domain with the probability range in @tbl-prospect-fourfold gives four recurring patterns under commonly used parameterizations.

Many decisions combine a statistical description and personal experience. A physician can read trial evidence and remember patients, while a resident can see a flood map and remember years without flooding. In @tbl-experience-states, check which source is available and how it was formed. If they conflict, investigate whether they cover the same outcomes and conditions.

Hertwig and Wulff (2022) organize risk situations by asking whether description and experience are present or absent. The responses in @tbl-experience-states follow from what is missing: a selective history calls for broader evidence, while a described distribution may need a clearer, more usable presentation.
The slowly falling one-percent curve in @fig-experience-rare-event-sampling shows why an uneventful sample can coexist with a real rare-event risk.

Reviewing the four cells in @tbl-process-outcome prevents a successful result from excusing a poor process or a bad result from condemning a sound one. Hindsight, self-serving attribution, and rationalization make this separation difficult. People can sincerely explain choices whose causes they did not notice (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977; Johansson et al., 2005), so a retrospective account needs something firmer than memory to compare with.

But a notional budget can become nonfungible. Someone may reject a worthwhile theatre ticket because the entertainment budget was used on a sports event, yet buy it after an equally costly medical expense or after receiving the sports ticket as a gift. Heath and Soll (1996) used such comparisons to show category-sensitive spending. @tbl-mental-budgets reports the study's **$50 prior-expense condition**. Each entry is the percentage showing the predicted “no after a prior purchase, yes after receiving that item as a gift, yes after an unrelated expense” pattern, averaged across four unrelated-expense controls.

In @fig-mental-accounting-evidence-redraw, the return horizon changes how the investment looks. The difference concerns hypothetical allocations between display conditions. The earlier brokerage comparison concerns subsequent returns on positions investors chose to sell or hold. Together they give separate reasons to check when an account feels closed and how often outcomes are evaluated.

A budget helps protect money for a purpose, yet the same boundary can make a worthwhile purchase seem unaffordable while funds sit elsewhere. The audit needs to preserve the useful protection and expose the costly restriction. Check whose goal the boundary serves, whether total cost and alternatives remain visible, and whether the chooser can revise it. A saving rule should protect a goal the household endorses; a seller benefits from a misleading boundary when it hides a cost or a feasible substitute. Use @tbl-mental-accounting-audit to reconstruct the decision twice, comparing the existing account with the alternatives and future costs that its boundary may hide:

The worked example in @fig-discount-model-crossover shows **dynamic inconsistency**: a plan that looks best from a distance can lose when temptation or effort becomes immediate. O'Donoghue and Rabin (1999) show how present bias can produce two familiar failures:
Compare the illustrative discount factors and the worked quasi-hyperbolic values in @fig-discount-factor-functions.

A delay raises different questions. What evidence would make the later payment credible? What would an ordinary day for the future beneficiary look like? Which first step could the person take now? Use @tbl-22-delay-mechanisms to find the question that changes the choice.

Before trying to make someone more patient, check whether the way the options are described changes the comparison. The classroom mnemonic **MOST** in @tbl-most-discounting keeps four option attributes visible, so that a change in wording or scale is not mistaken for a change in patience:
Make a choice from @tbl-hidden-zero-abbreviated before reading the second display.
Now compare the same options in @tbl-hidden-zero-complete. Would you keep your first choice?

A multiple price list seems to turn patience into a number: at which row does a person switch from a smaller-sooner to a larger-later amount? But choosing the earlier payment could also keep an urgent bill paid or avoid a promise the person distrusts. Treating either constraint as impatience would point to the wrong remedy. The design responses in @tbl-discount-identification show what must be measured or held comparable before attributing the observed choice to time preference.
Before choosing, use @tbl-intertemporal-time-stream to sketch what each option creates before, during, and after the focal event:

Lally and colleagues (2010) followed people repeating everyday actions in a consistent context. Their fitted curves could show diminishing gains in reported automaticity. The horizontal line in @fig-habit-formation-curve marks an analytical cutoff at 95% of an illustrative plateau.[^ch21-plateau]

The location of the signal matters. Peciña and Berridge (2005) found that mu-opioid stimulation increased eating across the accumbens shell, but enhanced positive reactions to sweetness only within a small hotspot. Wanting and liking therefore involve overlapping chemical systems with different functional effects. @tbl-wanting-liking summarizes the comparison.

Panels A–C of @fig-reward-prediction-error-shift show these three patterns. Panel D adds an unexpected delay: firing falls when the reward fails to arrive on time, then rises when it finally appears (Hollerman & Schultz, 1998). The dip reflects a violated expectation about timing. A delay known in advance creates a different expectation. Zero on these curves represents baseline firing, so a flat line at reward delivery can accompany enjoyment of a fully expected reward.

**A longer wait can reduce a reward's present value.** Kobayashi and Schultz (2008) trained two monkeys with cues predicting juice after different delays. Responses to the predictive cues declined as the delay increased, consistent with the animals' preference for sooner rewards. This was a known delay, unlike the unexpected lateness in panel D of @fig-reward-prediction-error-shift.

The classroom practice **BRAIN** gives the pause a simple structure: **Breathe, Recognize, Allow, Investigate, and Non-identify**.[^ch21-brain] Try it with a mild everyday urge, such as the student's wish for one more post. The prompts in @tbl-20-brain move from noticing the impulse to choosing a response.

@fig-reward-uncertainty-comparison contrasts a certain reward with a 50% chance of the same reward at the same time. The uncertain condition produces a smaller brief response to the cue, followed by increasing activity during the wait. Its two branches share that anticipatory history: firing rises if reward arrives and falls below baseline if it is omitted. The outcome determines which branch occurs.

In @tbl-two-working-lives, compare the two jobs on a representative Tuesday before asking how you would evaluate that choice afterward. Thinking about the salary, living through a day and remembering the move later can give different answers. The six measurement questions below distinguish those answers.

What people remember can also influence what they choose to repeat. In a cold-water experiment, participants experienced a painful 60-second immersion and a longer immersion with the same first minute followed by 30 seconds in gradually warming, still unpleasant water. As @fig-cold-water-better-ending shows, the longer trial added discomfort but improved the ending. Twenty-two of the 32 men in the analyzed student sample chose to repeat it (Kahneman et al., 1993). Peaks and endings can thus shape a later choice even when they give an incomplete account of the time lived through.

Experience sampling asks about feelings at selected moments. The Day Reconstruction Method asks people to reconstruct yesterday’s episodes and the feelings associated with them (Kahneman et al., 2004). Both capture aspects of daily experience, and reconstruction draws on memory.[^ch22-affect-measurement] @tbl-well-being-targets shows which question each measure can answer.

Having followed the job through prediction, choice, experience, and reflection, use @tbl-well-being-targets to keep the questions separate. A strong answer in one row cannot silently stand in for the others.
The contrasts in @tbl-relational-well-being prevent the amount of contact from standing in for its quality or the support it provides:

Killingsworth (2021) asked employed US adults to rate how they felt at sampled moments on a continuous scale. Average experienced well-being continued to rise beyond the earlier threshold. @tbl-income-wellbeing-measures makes the measurement difference explicit.

The jobs can rank differently on pay, daily experience, purpose, and relationships. A single overall impression can hide which sacrifice produces the apparent advantage. Compare the options across the four fields in @tbl-well-being-decision-audit so that gains in one area can be weighed against sacrifices in another and checked at the later review. Complete one line in each cell; add detail only where it could change the decision.
@tbl-beauty-contest-groups reproduces selected guessing-game results from their Table II. The fitted $\tau$ values in this table were chosen to match the observed mean.
Buyers and sellers can stand to gain from trade yet fail to find acceptable terms. Compare @tbl-market-institutions: each rule changes who can act, what they observe, and how a price forms.

To isolate the choice of destination, suppose each of you goes to either the main entrance or the information desk and waits there. Assume that you find each other if you choose the same place, and set aside differences in walking distance or the view of the performance. Represent a successful meeting with 50 illustrative payoff units for each person and a failed meeting with zero. The **payoff matrix** in @tbl-meeting-coordination records what each receives under every combination of choices.
The distinction builds through the levels in @tbl-private-mutual-common-knowledge. Here *X* stands for a fact.

The **stag hunt** isolates this problem (Skyrms, 2004). Two hunters can secure the larger return only by hunting stag together. Each can instead hunt hare independently. In the illustrative payoff matrix in @tbl-stag-hunt, the first number belongs to Player 1.

In @fig-stag-hunt-belief-payoffs, Hare's payoff stays at 10 while Stag's expected payoff rises with confidence in the partner. Their crossing shows why wanting the better joint outcome is not enough to make Stag the best individual choice.
The reporting dispute can now be separated into actionable problems. The rows of @tbl-strategic-structures identify obstacles that can coexist; each suggests a different first intervention.

After specifying the game, keep the answers supplied by equilibrium analysis separate from questions that require evidence about the people involved. @tbl-equilibrium-boundary collects that distinction: identifying a stable combination is one step in evaluating a joint decision.

The illustrative price-war matrix in @tbl-price-war shows the distinction. Its numbers represent profit units and omit many features of an actual market. Rao and colleagues (2000) examine how responses to price competition depend on such details of the competitive setting.

The colleagues choose simultaneously whether to share their notes. @tbl-one-shot-pd represents sharing as Cooperate and withholding as Defect. Its illustrative payoffs combine the benefit of receiving useful input and the cost of providing it.
@tbl-preference-norm separates these expectations from private preferences and enforcement. Its purpose is to keep an observed act of helping from being treated as a complete explanation of itself.

@tbl-cooperation-mechanisms collects the conditions examined in this chapter. They can coexist: a continuing relationship can also have a reputation system and formal enforcement. Each changes the reason cooperation might be chosen.

The comparison in @tbl-three-strategic-lenses makes the object of explanation explicit. A population can change because existing members revise what they do, because some members are replaced, or because the rules of the interaction change. None of these possibilities can be inferred from a final pattern alone.

One recurring condition supporting cooperation is **positive assortment**: cooperators encounter cooperators more often than random mixing would predict. The model must explain how this pattern arises. @tbl-five-rules separates how relatedness, repeated encounters, reputation, and population structure can support cooperation (Nowak, 2006).

Suppose sharing notes becomes common across teams. Employees may repeat it after a useful return, copy respected colleagues, or comply with a new rule. Alternatively, teams that share may attract resources and expand while other teams disappear. @tbl-strategy-diffusion-diagnostic separates changes within continuing units from changes in which units remain.

Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler (1986) asked separate samples of respondents to judge market practices. @fig-fairness-entitlements-redraw shows four selected historical vignettes. The car questions hold the size of the price increase at $200 but vary its relation to list price: one adds a surcharge above list, while the other removes a discount below list.[^ch25-fairness-vignettes]

Asch-type conformity varies across periods, cultures, tasks, and response conditions (Bond & Smith, 1996). In @fig-asch-line-comparison, which comparison line matches the target? Make your own judgment, then imagine that everyone before you publicly answered B. Consider whether this would change your private belief, your public response, or both.
The committee’s nods illustrate the distinction in @tbl-social-alignment-mechanisms: learning something and withholding a doubt can produce the same public agreement.

Before reading @tbl-private-public-judgments, ask what another public vote could reveal. Committee A’s private judgments changed. Ask which independent evidence, if any, members learned and how it changed their forecasts. Committee B’s members kept their judgments but changed what they said publicly. Ask what speaking up would have cost and which protected way of recording disagreement would reveal it. These comparisons can help distinguish learning from pressure. Both can operate in one group.

In the first experiment, both conditions used randomly ordered grids. In the second, the independent list remained randomly ordered, while the social lists ranked songs by downloads. The example menus in @fig-cultural-market-study-redraw make the changing information and order visible.
Use @tbl-22-1 to audit the cue behind an apparent consensus before treating the consensus as additional evidence.
@fig-mimicry-study-redraw compares behavior under different partner conditions. The face-rubbing contrast was stronger than the foot-shaking contrast.
The two figures in @fig-personal-mimicry-crossed-arms stand several metres apart with their arms crossed. The photograph shows what the two postures look like together.

In @fig-finance-fed-announcement, the S&P 500 moves sharply at the announcement. The relevant comparison for a trader is the price available after learning the news, not the earlier price visible on the chart. An order submitted after reading and interpreting the announcement cannot retrospectively capture that initial jump.

The space shuttle *Challenger* exploded at 11:39 a.m. on January 28, 1986; a Dow Jones newswire report followed at 11:47. All four major publicly traded contractors initially lost value. In @fig-finance-challenger, however, Morton Thiokol separates from the others. Measured from the previous day’s close, its stock fell 11.86%, compared with declines of roughly 2–3% for Lockheed, Martin Marietta, and Rockwell. Months later, the presidential commission identified failure of the booster O-ring seals supplied by Thiokol (Maloney & Mulherin, 2003).

Rendleman, Jones, and Latané (1982) grouped companies by standardized unexpected quarterly earnings. In @fig-finance-earnings-evidence, the more favorable surprises are associated with higher cumulative abnormal returns. A reader may follow Sara closely and still leave without understanding how to change a meeting. Another may remember her embarrassment while forgetting the information that challenged her belief. Compare Africa and Greenland in @fig-communication-projections. A globe keeps their curved surfaces in proportion. Greenland can look as large as Africa even though Africa is about fourteen times its area. **Gall–Peters** preserves relative area, so that difference is visible, but it stretches or flattens shapes.

The first task is to identify what kind of response the conversation needs at this moment. The same sentence can carry at least three kinds of need. A **practical** conversation asks what to do. An **emotional** conversation asks for recognition, regulation, or company. A **social or identity** conversation asks what the event says about respect, belonging, competence, fairness, or the relationship (Duhigg, 2024; Stone et al., 2010). These are practical prompts for listening, not three experimentally established kinds of conversation. The layers in @tbl-29-conversation-layer connect possible needs to opening questions. Advice can miss a request for understanding, while recognition alone can leave an urgent problem unresolved.

When direct bargaining stalls, bringing in a third party can seem like the obvious next step. Yet the parties may want help finding their own agreement or need a final decision they cannot reach together. Choosing a process without resolving that difference can surrender control when assistance was intended, or prolong the dispute when finality was needed. A third party can repair a process or replace it. The mediation–arbitration distinction in @tbl-34-third-party-processes follows the allocation of authority used in the UNCITRAL frameworks (UNCITRAL, 2022).

A reminder about a free workplace flu clinic already tells employees where and when vaccination is available. Would asking them to choose their own visit time add anything? Milkman and colleagues (2011) randomly assigned employees to a basic reminder or one prompting them to write a planned date and time. Workplace vaccination was 33.1% with the basic reminder and 37.1% with the planning prompt. The raw difference in @fig-vaccination-plans is 4.0 percentage points; adjusting for employee characteristics gave 4.2 points (95% confidence interval: 0.5–7.8). A separate date-only condition at sites with multiday clinics did not reliably outperform the basic reminder.

An **investment** is effort that makes a later visit more valuable or sets up another cue. Saving an explanation creates useful material to return to; posting a follow-up question may generate the next reply alert (Eyal, 2014). In the student's writing routine, leaving notes and a selected comparison prepares the next start. Variable rewards and investment can thus support repetition, but neither is required for every habit: reliable, satisfying progress can also encourage return. @tbl-21-digital-loop examines when these features support the user's goal and when they make disengagement difficult.

The four targets in @fig-bias-and-noise separate the location and spread of comparable judgments around an observed or accepted benchmark. **Level noise** is persistent variation in judges' average severity or generosity. **Pattern noise** concerns differences in reactions to particular cases. It has two components: **stable pattern noise**, such as a judge consistently giving unusual weight to a case feature, and **occasion noise**, variation in the same judge’s response across times or contexts. Estimate level noise, stable pattern noise, and occasion noise with a repeated-judgment design (Kahneman et al., 2021, ch. 16).

Data analysis is the systematic use of observations to answer a question. **Descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics** distinguish four purposes, not four products or mutually exclusive techniques (INFORMS, n.d.). The same records can serve several purposes. In @tbl-four-uses-of-data, Flint provides a common setting so that the change in question is easy to see.

Evaluation should match the analytical purpose. A descriptive report needs accurate definitions, denominators, and coverage. A diagnostic explanation must address competing accounts; a causal claim needs a defensible comparison. A prediction needs testing on relevant new cases. A prescription needs evaluation against the objective, constraints, costs, and consequences of the action. These checks build on the distinctions in @tbl-four-uses-of-data.

Expected loss weights each possible error by its probability: 70% for dry weather and 30% for rain. The comparison in @tbl-ai-rain-losses favors moving indoors for the first organizer and remaining outdoors for the second. Neither needs a different weather forecast. They face different consequences.

With these hypothetical losses, the thresholds in @fig-ai-same-forecast-different-values are 20 percent and 60 percent, placing the same 30 percent forecast on opposite sides of the action threshold. At equality, the model leaves the organizer indifferent. A threshold of 50 percent would be appropriate only for equal error losses under these assumptions.
The distinctions in @tbl-ai-flint-decision show what turns the probability map into a programme: an objective, feasible actions, operating constraints, and authority to decide and review.

Consider the two hypothetical groups in @fig-ai-risk-is-not-benefit. Without outreach, their expected dropout rates are 60 and 40 percent. Suppose valid intervention evidence suggested rates of 55 and 20 percent with outreach. The expected reductions would be 5 and 20 percentage points. Ranking only baseline risk would prioritize the first group; ranking expected benefit per equal-cost place, with equal value assigned to each prevented dropout, would prioritize the second.

Suppose the city asks a team to “use AI” to improve pipe replacement. One member proposes a risk model, another a chatbot to answer residents' questions, and a third a scheduling tool for crews. Each addresses a different obstacle. The four analytical purposes help the team identify which obstacle matters before choosing a tool. The workbench in @tbl-ai-workbench includes ordinary reporting and causal analysis alongside predictive models, language models, retrieval systems, and optimizers. A workflow can combine them, with a different check for each output.

Use @tbl-ai-decision-canvas to specify the decision, missing evidence, protected values, and review rule before selecting a product or writing a prompt. The separate fields make it possible to judge the tool by the contribution the decision actually needs.

Before judging whether a preference serves the person well, distinguish four questions. How strongly does the person favor an outcome, what experience follows, what evolutionary history is proposed, and what ought they to pursue? @tbl-fitness-utility-welfare-morality keeps these questions separate, so that an explanation of a preference is not mistaken for a reason to endorse it:

The comparison in @tbl-maslow-popular-kenrick shows why the popular pyramid cannot stand in for either theoretical proposal. Keep three questions separate when using these accounts: when a motive develops, what activates it now, and what historical function is proposed for it. Those are different claims even when they concern the same behavior.

A quick choice of food might be consistent with a person's preference, sensible given limited time, and unhelpful for a long-term health goal. The standards in @tbl-rationality-standards can therefore produce different assessments of the same choice: consistency, feasible effort, and fit to the environment are distinct criteria. [Appendix A](appendix-a-rational-choice-and-decision-analysis.qmd) develops the formal benchmark. Here the task is to keep its purpose distinct from ecological and evolutionary questions.

A familiar cue can make a good shortcut when it tracks the outcome we care about. If the relationship changes, the same shortcut can mislead. The recognition and availability examples in @tbl-heuristics-fit-and-failure show why evaluation must specify which cues track the target and what could break that relationship.

A coherent evolutionary story can make a puzzling preference seem explained. Yet learning, current incentives, or cultural transmission might fit the same observation. Accepting the first plausible story would leave us unable to predict when the preference should change. An evolutionary account earns confidence by predicting evidence that distinguishes it from those alternatives. @tbl-evolutionary-evidence separates what each source of evidence can establish from the historical claims it leaves open.

Return to the invitation to give a prestigious talk from Chapter 6. Its prestige makes acceptance appealing, but accepting also commits time that could serve other priorities. Calling the attraction a status motive explains little about whether to accept. The useful question is what prestige predicts here and how those consequences fit the person's commitments. The questions in @tbl-evolutionary-valuation-audit unpack the attraction before asking whether to act on it:

The proposed sequence in @tbl-bennett-five-breakthroughs suggests an expansion in the sources from which choice can learn: inherited valence, the consequences of one's own actions, internally simulated futures, observed agents and inferred minds, and culturally communicated experience. Later capacities do not replace earlier ones. Human deliberation still depends on approach and avoidance, reinforcement, and embodied action; language and culture can redirect those systems rather than float above them.

Imagine two inherited beetle types competing for food. Large beetles gain an advantage against small ones but need more food to sustain their bodies. The invented payoffs in @tbl-beetle-arms-race represent reproductive weights after that cost. They illustrate a possible mechanism; they are not measurements of beetles.

Now suppose aggressive behavior gains against a yielding opponent but becomes costly when both escalate. In the illustrative **hawk–dove** game in @tbl-hawk-dove-weights, all payoffs are nonnegative weights, with background reproduction already included.

Spatial models add another dependency: who interacts with whom. Cooperative clusters, conditional helping, or aggregate segregation can arise under particular neighborhoods and update rules. The record in @tbl-model-provenance makes these dependencies explicit, so another reader can reconstruct the result and assess how far it applies:

@fig-schelling-emergence applies that standard. In one seeded Schelling-style teaching run, agents move only when fewer than one-third of their occupied neighbours share their group and choose a vacancy satisfying that threshold. The average same-group-neighbour share rises from 0.48 to 0.68.
Keep the record in @tbl-literature-search-record as you work. It lets a reader understand the scope and lets you recover a decision you might otherwise forget.

The fields in @tbl-literature-evidence-matrix keep the study’s design, result, and role in the review distinct. Use one row per study, adding separate rows for materially different experiments or outcomes and marking shared samples. Record enough detail to reconstruct a claim, without copying every result into the review.

The selected studies in @tbl-positive-thinking-review-example show why a synthesis needs more than a list of favorable and unfavorable results. Compare what each study measures or changes before deciding whether its finding answers the same question.

Draft from the question and evidence matrix. Use @tbl-literature-review-structure to give each section a job in answering the question, then write paragraphs that make an interpretable claim, examine its support, and explain what the comparison adds. Revise the introduction once you know the answer so that it promises the review you actually deliver.
The three selected studies in @tbl-savings-review-example compare how saving changes under different interventions.

The five phases in @tbl-experimental-workflow turn the clinic's question into a study whose decisions and results can be examined. Each leaves a record needed to interpret the next: the question determines the comparison, the design determines what must be recorded, and those records determine which conclusion the analysis can support.

Use @tbl-experimental-workflow to start filling out the clinic’s record. Specify an administrative attendance measure, compare two assigned reminder groups and record missing outcomes by group. A gap in the attendance record limits what the comparison can answer even when assignment worked.

Choose one claim from the book or current media. Use @tbl-experimental-workflow to specify the question, construct, measure, comparison, estimand, and final sentence. Identify the weakest step, then propose a redesign or narrow the claim to what the comparison can establish.

With the outcome defined, return to the question the study is meant to answer. @tbl-claim-families connects each kind of claim to the comparison or check it requires, preventing an accurate prediction from being mistaken for evidence about an intervention.

@tbl-evidence-designs compares approaches by what generates the contrast and what assumptions support it. Start with that process: an experiment, a naturally occurring difference, and a simulated outcome provide different grounds for inference.

Follow the two forks in @fig-random-sampling-vs-assignment. The first determines who enters the evaluation; the second determines which condition those participants are assigned to. The control group is part of the evaluation sample and must be followed for outcomes. People outside the evaluation are not that control group. The figure shows one possible design: a trial can use random assignment without random sampling, as in the volunteer example above, while requiring a separate argument about generalization.

The markets receiving no offers were deliberately included and measured as **pure controls**. They are different from the people outside the evaluation in @fig-random-sampling-vs-assignment. Higher-level assignment, buffer areas, or network measurement may also help, but none should be treated as proof that interference has disappeared. State whose outcome depends on whose treatment and whether the study estimates an individual gain, an effect on others, or a broader policy effect.

Suppose the clinic establishes that its new reminder improves attendance. A neighboring clinic wants to adopt it, but serves patients with different needs and uses a different booking system. The original comparison cannot by itself tell that clinic what to expect. The sampling step in @fig-random-sampling-vs-assignment supports inference to a defined population; extending the result to a different setting requires examining what else has changed.

2. Trace a patient through @fig-random-sampling-vs-assignment. Explain how being outside the evaluation differs from assignment to its control group, and when household assignment might be preferable.

In @tbl-clinic-assignment-flow, compare receipt and observation separately. Some assigned messages did not arrive. Some attendance outcomes are missing. The outcome totals therefore tell us neither the exact number who received a message and were observed nor what happened to patients with missing records. Keep patients grouped by original assignment for the intention-to-treat analysis and address missing outcomes explicitly. A further comparison asks whether a patient who receives a reminder tells a household member about the appointment. The household member’s outcome can then depend on another person’s assignment.

The school-meal exercise in @tbl-school-meals-noncompliance uses invented changes in reading scores to separate assignment from participation. Ten pupils belong to a school assigned meals and ten to a comparison school; some pupils in each school receive meals. Every pupil's score change is observed.

Use @tbl-research-reactivity to identify which pathways your design needs to address. A systematic review found highly varied evidence under the Hawthorne label, with substantial uncertainty about mechanisms and magnitudes (McCambridge et al., 2014). More specifically, Zwane and colleagues (2011) randomly varied survey exposure across five field studies: surveys increased use of health products in three studies, but the two microlending studies did not detect changes in borrowing. Measurement can matter without having one predictable effect everywhere.

@tbl-claim-design-matching shows how wording can preserve or exceed what a design establishes. In particular, an effect of assignment should not become a claim about everyone who receives treatment, and a modeled pattern should not become proof of a human mechanism.

Complete @tbl-evidence-design-card before collecting data. Reading across the fields should reveal whether the measure, comparison, analysis, and intended claim fit together; an unresolved entry identifies a design decision that still needs attention.

@tbl-worked-reminder-design fixes the reminder comparison, attendance outcome, and analysis before the result is known. The data below are generated with a declared seed and fixed probabilities solely to make that workflow reproducible:

Return to the [clinic reminder study in Appendix D](appendix-e-how-behavioral-evidence-is-built.qmd#running-an-experimental-study-from-question-to-credible-evidence). In @tbl-clinic-evidence-audit follow one attendance comparison and check which records let a reader see how it was produced. Preregistration gives a plan to compare with the report. Code makes a calculation inspectable. Replication supplies new evidence.

Use @tbl-clinic-evidence-audit to find where the comparisons became less informative. Ask what was measured, which results were selected, and what the replication examined. Propose the next study, the claim that the evidence currently supports and one change that would make the record easier to interpret.

A claim that a finding has been “checked” sounds reassuring. Reproducing its calculation, however, can leave an incorrect measure or a confounded comparison intact. Before relying on the finding, use the distinctions in @tbl-credibility-questions to ask which source of uncertainty the check actually addressed.

@fig-selected-literature-simulation isolates one mechanism. The generator uses independent normal-outcome studies with true effect 0.20 standard deviations, outcome variance 1, 50 observations per arm, and seed 20260830. A known-variance, two-sided z test with alpha .05 gives each difference in means standard error 0.20 and theoretical power 17.0%. The significance-only rule makes 328 of 2,000 studies visible; their mean estimate is 0.490, about 2.5 times the true effect, and four have the wrong sign. The deterministic generator is `scripts/build_methods_appendix_figures.py`; its study-level output and parameter record are preserved in `figures/source/selected-literature-simulation.csv` and `.json`.

Choose among the safeguards in @tbl-research-safeguards according to the problem each can address. Recording an analysis plan makes later changes visible; sharing code makes calculations inspectable. Neither alone establishes that the outcome measures what the researcher intended.

Read @tbl-famous-direct-replication-cases across each row, from the original claim to the later test or integrity update. A result that was not reproduced and a retraction change confidence for different reasons; the table keeps the tested procedure and the broader interpretation distinct.

The cases in @tbl-famous-qualified-replication-cases belong in the same teaching map because they are often described casually as “debunked.” That label discards the most useful information: what changed and what remains.
In @tbl-canonical-tools, start with the task in the first column, follow the tool link to its instructions, and use the final column to check what your completed record should contain.

If the outcome is still unknown, the **One-Page Decision Journal** helps preserve your reasoning. If you are reviewing a completed decision, the **Decision Audit Studio** helps separate the process from the result. Use @tbl-tool-levels to match the depth of the tool to the stakes and the record you need. Add another tool only when the first reveals a question it cannot answer. Each box is labelled by its role below; a quick check can start a discussion, but consequential decisions may require a fuller record.

Use the same seven labels in @tbl-portable-decision-journal at both moments. Read across each row: the entry after the outcome must answer the question recorded before choosing, so hindsight cannot silently replace the original reasoning.
Use @tbl-tactic-diagnostic to separate what a bargaining move may be trying to signal from the evidence you need before responding.
Use @tbl-recurring-case-map to follow how a familiar case takes on a new question, such as moving from a supplier’s refusal to the terms that make an agreement workable.

The **Evidence role** column in @tbl-extended-example-index distinguishes fictional illustrations, reported cases, and research studies, so that a memorable example is not mistaken for an empirical test. Use the chapter links to recover the comparison and limits behind an example before reusing it.

The chapter links and viewing questions in @tbl-linked-video-cases give each optional clip a specific job. Use the clip to examine that question, then return to the chapter's evidence before drawing a general conclusion. If a link is unavailable, the question can guide a replacement scene or written case.
